item.base_system: NbTaTiV refractory high-entropy alloy (nominal Nb25Ta25Ti25V25 at%)
item.intervention: Homogenization treatment at 1200°C for 3 days followed by water cooling
item.processing: Arc melting under argon atmosphere, drop-casting into 4-mm diameter rods, sealed in quartz tubes, homogenized at 1200°C for 3 days, water cooled
item.structure_change: Formation of a single BCC solid solution with grain sizes of 200 to 400 μm, no secondary phases or elemental segregations
item.property_change: Excellent phase stability of the single BCC phase up to 900°C
item.attributed_mechanism: Minimization of Gibbs free energy by increasing configurational entropy results in the formation of a single-phase solid solution
quotes: A typical simple solid-solution HEA microstructure with grain sizes of 200 to 400 μm was identified without the presence of secondary phases or elemental segregations.
The single BCC phase is stable up to 900°C, indicating the excellent phase stability at elevated temperatures.

records.text: Intervention effect. Base system: NbTaTiV refractory high-entropy alloy (nominal Nb25Ta25Ti25V25 at%). Intervention: Homogenization treatment at 1200°C for 3 days followed by water cooling. Processing: Arc melting under argon atmosphere, drop-casting into 4-mm diameter rods, sealed in quartz tubes, homogenized at 1200°C for 3 days, water cooled. Test conditions: Room temperature (RT) and elevated temperatures (500°C, 700°C, 900°C). Structure change: Formation of a single BCC solid solution with grain sizes of 200 to 400 μm, no secondary phases or elemental segregations. Property change: Excellent phase stability of the single BCC phase up to 900°C. Mechanism: Minimization of Gibbs free energy by increasing configurational entropy results in the formation of a single-phase solid solution. Evidence: measured. Quote: "A typical simple solid-solution HEA microstructure with grain sizes of 200 to 400 μm was identified without the presence of secondary phases or elemental segregations."

item.intervention: In situ neutron diffraction compression tests at strain rate of 1 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹
item.processing: Compression experiments on 4 mm diameter x 8 mm length samples using a mechanical testing system load frame
item.structure_change: Lattice strain evolution showed no clear variation in diffraction elastic constants among grains at RT
item.property_change: Yield strength decreased from 1064 MPa (RT) to 595 MPa (900°C); work-hardening exponent decreased from 0.2732 (RT) to 0.1199 (900°C)
item.attributed_mechanism: The random distribution of multiple elements leads to a severely distorted lattice, contributing to unique deformation behaviors
quotes: The yield strength (σ y ) and work-hardening exponent ( N ) of the present alloy gradually decreased from 1064 MPa (RT) to 595 MPa (900°C) and from 0.2732 (RT) to 0.1199 (900°C), respectively.
It was found that the variation in diffraction elastic constants among all the grains is not clearly observed, indicating the elastically isotropic deformation behavior, as presented in Fig. 2A .

item.intervention: Temperature increase from RT to 900°C during compression
item.processing: In situ neutron diffraction with compression tests
item.structure_change: Different slopes in lattice strains versus applied stresses observed at elevated temperatures due to increased elastic anisotropy
item.property_change: Elastic anisotropy gradually increases at elevated temperatures, but the variation is not notable compared to conventional alloys
item.attributed_mechanism: At higher temperatures, where the overall stiffness is reduced, the anisotropy increases
quotes: Unlike the lattice strain evolution at RT, different slopes in the lattice strains versus applied stresses at elevated temperatures are observed due to the increased elastic anisotropy, as presented in Fig. 2 (B to D) .

item.intervention: Application of Kroner, Voigt, and Reuss models to diffraction elastic moduli
item.processing: Theoretical modeling of macroscopic elastic moduli from experimental lattice strain data
item.structure_change: Kroner model showed best agreement with experimental data (absolute percentage SEs of 2.46% at RT, 8.85% at 900°C)
item.property_change: Tetragonal shear modulus (C′) substantially reduced with decreasing elastic, shear, and bulk moduli up to 700°C
item.attributed_mechanism: The Kroner model accounts for the variation of stresses and strains among all the grains
quotes: The results, as exhibited in Fig. 2 (E to H) , indicate that the Kroner model is in the best agreement with the experimental data for all temperature ranges, as compared to the Voigt and Reuss models.

item.processing: Vienna Ab-initio Simulation Package (VASP) with PAW method, 64-atom SQS, 700 eV cutoff, 4×4×4 k-point grid
item.structure_change: Calculated elastic constant values for C11, C12, and C′ all decrease from absolute zero to RT
item.property_change: Calculated elastic moduli at RT were less than experimentally measured values by approximately −15.9% (Young's), −16.6% (shear), and −6.0% (bulk)
item.attributed_mechanism: The above result corroborates the general trend of decreased stiffness in metals with increasing temperature
quotes: The calculated elastic moduli at RT were less than the experimentally measured values by approximately −15.9, −16.6, and −6.0% for the Young's, shear, and bulk moduli, respectively.

item.intervention: Machine Learning (ML) model training on Materials Project database
item.processing: Gradient-boosted trees algorithm using scikit-learn, trained on 80% of 6826 compounds, 5-fold cross-validation
item.structure_change: Model predictions for shear and bulk moduli converged after 3000 training samples
item.property_change: Predicted shear modulus 36.6 GPa (2.5% error) and bulk modulus 146.3 GPa (6% error) compared to experimental values
item.attributed_mechanism: The good agreement suggests that these models may be useful for conservative estimates despite the lack of disordered alloy data in the database
quotes: The predicted shear modulus is 36.6 GPa, and the predicted bulk modulus is 146.3 GPa, giving relative errors of 2.5 and 6%, respectively.
